title: MACaQ: Fast, Model Agnostic Calibrated Quantization for Low-Precision Weights and Activations
why: If the self-reported numbers hold, you can quantize a 122B-parameter model to 4-bit weights and activations in 64 minutes on a single 32.5GB GPU, with only 2.3% inference overhead over plain MXFP4.
notes: MACaQ is an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently, avoiding the cross-layer basis-transform propagation that other recent methods require.

Each layer gets a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform applied to activations online at inference; the inverse transforms are folded into the weights. Keeping transforms online removes cross-layer dependencies and permits a streaming implementation holding only one layer in memory at a time.
Flip-Refinement is a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent step that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values, improving over round-to-nearest.

Reported results: 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM; lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, matching their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11x less quantization time; a 122B model quantized in 64 minutes using 32.5GB GPU RAM.
The same layer-local design is applied to an image diffusion model without architecture-specific changes, which the authors offer as evidence of generality.
All numbers are author-reported from the arXiv abstract; no independent evaluation, methodology detail, or baseline configuration is provided in the excerpt.
summary: MACaQ is a post-training quantization method for MXFP4 W4A4 (4-bit weights and activations) that quantizes each linear layer independently, in contrast to methods that propagate basis transforms across layers. It applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform to activations online at inference time and absorbs the inverse transforms into the weights; because transforms stay online rather than being fused across layers, quantization can stream through the model with only one layer resident in memory. A Flip-Refinement step uses Hessian-aware coordinate descent to move individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values, improving on round-to-nearest. The authors report 2.3% end-to-end inference overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM, lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, matching their best Llama-3-8B perplexity in 11x less quantization time, and quantization of a 122B-parameter model in 64 minutes using 32.5GB of GPU RAM. The method is also applied unmodified to an image diffusion model. All figures are self-reported in the abstract and lack independent verification or methodology detail.
novelty: layer-local online Hadamard quantization avoids cross-layer calibration

title: Switch Lowering in GCC
why: If you have ever profiled a hot dispatch loop and wondered why GCC emitted branches instead of a jump table, this reverse-engineers the exact thresholds that decide it, down to a ratio of 8 at -O3 versus 2 at -Os.
notes: The jump-table heuristic compares jump-table entries against comparisons, not raw case labels: GCC merges contiguous case ranges first, so a 20-label switch spanning 0-87 (88 entries) lowers to comparisons because it reduces to 10 comparisons and 10*8 < 88 fails the ratio test.

The ratio is set by optimization goal: 8 entries-per-comparison when optimizing for speed (-O1/2/3/fast), 2 when optimizing for size (-Os). Both bitset and jump-table lowering use dynamic programming to minimize the number of clusters.

For small, non-contiguous value sets GCC emits a bitset plus the x86 bt (bit test) instruction against a constant (e.g. 2753205), where set bits are the ASCII case values each offset by 48; the author notes bitset lowering does not transfer to Clang.

GCC detects dense subsets inside sparse switches: an outlier like case 100 gets its own cmp/branch while cases 1-5 still get a jump table. Jump tables below case_values_threshold (defaults to 5 on modern x64/Arm64) are pruned as unprofitable.

Missed optimization flagged by the author: in a sparse-but-regular switch (sparse_8), GCC does not divide x by 8 before indexing, emitting a comparison tree instead. The fallback tree is built by splitting labels into equal-probability halves, using PGO or __builtin_expect_with_probability.
The work is attributed to the pass_lower_switch pass calling analyze_switch_statement, observed under GCC -O3 from disassembly; findings are the author's reverse-engineering, not GCC documentation.
summary: A reverse-engineering walkthrough of how GCC lowers C switch statements, derived from -O3 disassembly and annotated GCC source. GCC chooses among three strategies: a jump table (indirect jump through an address array), a bitset test using the bt instruction for small non-contiguous value sets, and a binary decision tree as fallback. The jump-table decision uses dynamic programming and a ratio heuristic comparing jump-table entries to the number of comparisons after contiguous ranges are merged, with the ratio being 8 for speed and 2 for size; jump tables smaller than case_values_threshold (default 5) are rejected. GCC can isolate dense subsets within sparse switches, emitting a table for the cluster and separate branches for outliers. The author notes missed optimizations, such as failing to divide the index by a stride in a regular-but-sparse case, and that all techniques except bitset lowering carry over to Clang.
novelty: reverse-engineers GCC's switch-lowering heuristics via disassembly
audience: systems/compiler engineers optimizing hot-path switch statements

title: The Commodore 64 hardware simulator: break chips and pins, see the results
why: If you repair vintage boards, this lets you reproduce a specific fault, lifting A7 on the color RAM, shorting a pin to +5V, pulling a chip, and read the resulting screen garbage before you desolder anything, so you touch the fewest chips in the most logical order.
notes: Simulates the Commodore 64 ASSY 250407 motherboard pin by pin from bwack's KiCad replica netlist: 216 parts, their pads, and 249 nets (converted by tools/kicad2c.py).

Cycle-accurate 6510/VIC-II/CIA/SID cores come from floooh's chips library (via c64-llm, zlib); antirez added pin-level models for the DRAMs, ROMs, color RAM, glue logic, and the PLA with its real 82S100 equations (read out by Mark Smith and Marko Mäkelä).

Not an emulator for play: it runs at 31% of real C64 speed on an Apple M3 Max, 39% on a Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495, and 48% on an Apple M5 Max, because every pin of every chip is simulated. Each half cycle settles in three steps: row address, /RAS falls, /CAS falls.

Electrical model: strongest drive wins a net, equal fighting drives show contention (low wins, magenta on the probe), undriven nets hold charge then drift to ~1.4V with TTL loads or toward 0V with MOS loads. A chip without GND floats its outputs high; a CMOS chip keeps running on phantom power through its pins' protection diodes. Noise is seeded so runs are reproducible.

Scriptable: CLI fault syntax REF:what or REF.PIN:what (U17:removed, U21.14:gnd, R51:open), --headless with --text reading the screen as a person would plus --shot PNG, timed --at faults, and tests/faults.sh covers 31 common faults whose expected symptoms were written down before the simulator ran. Author warns a matching symptom is a clue, not proof.

Stated limits: floating/power thresholds, drift times, and crosstalk are hand-tuned guesses in src/sim.c; video output, SID filter, PSU, and dot-clock PLL are not simulated; in-chip faults (bad DRAM cells, slow parts) and net-to-net bridges are planned but not implemented.
summary: c64-hw-sim is a pin-level simulator of the Commodore 64 ASSY 250407 motherboard by antirez, built to diagnose faults rather than play games. It combines floooh's cycle-accurate 6510/VIC-II/CIA/SID cores (zlib) with new pin-level models of the DRAMs, ROMs, color RAM, glue logic, and the PLA's real equations, driven by bwack's KiCad replica netlist (216 parts, 249 nets). The user can lift a chip leg, short a pin to GND or +5V, pull a chip, or open a resistor, and observe the computed result on the monitor, keyboard, and an on-screen oscilloscope; the garbage shown is derived from the circuit and net-level electrical rules (drive strength, contention, charge drift to ~1.4V or 0V, phantom CMOS power via protection diodes), not hand-authored. It runs well below real time (31-48% on an M3 Max, Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495, and M5 Max) and supports headless, scripted fault injection with text and screenshot output, plus a test suite of 31 faults with symptoms documented beforehand. The author is explicit that a matching symptom is a clue rather than proof, that floating and power thresholds are tuned guesses, and that the video output, SID filter, PSU, dot-clock PLL, in-chip faults, and net bridges are not modeled. It runs on macOS and Linux via OpenGL, sokol, and nuklear.
novelty: pin-level C64 motherboard simulator for fault diagnosis, not emulation
audience: retrocomputing hobbyists and hardware repair engineers
